# T3 Code

T3 Code is a minimal GUI for coding agents. A Node WebSocket server wraps provider CLIs and agents (Codex, Claude Code, Cursor, Grok, OpenCode, Antigravity) and serves web, desktop, and mobile clients.

You can think of T3 Code as an open source "bring-your-own-subscription" alternative to apps like Claude Desktop, Codex App, Cursor Glass and Conductor.

## What makes T3 Code special?

We have over 500,000 users who love T3 Code. It's important we maintain the things they love as we continue to iterate on the product. Here's a brief list of the things we can never compromise on.

### 1. Open at the core

T3 Code is truly open. We share our roadmap, we share how we think about things, and of course we share all our code. A large number of our users run forks. We work in the open, and should strive to stay that way.

### 2. Performance without compromise

Lots of apps have gotten bogged down with bad tech decisions and "slop". We have not, and we're proud of the performance of T3 Code. We regularly audit for performance regressions, often caused by sending too much data over websockets, css animations causing gpu spikes, lists being hard to render, and more. Make sure all changes are considerate of performance impact.

### 3. Remote ready

The architecture of T3 Code's websocket layer (npx t3) enables a lot of awesome remote features. These have become core to the product. Whether users are connecting directly over their local network, using Tailscale, or leaning in fully with T3 Connect (our tunnel solution, also in this repo), we need to make sure new features are properly supported.

### 4. Multi-surface

T3 Code has 3 key app surfaces: **web**, **desktop**, and **mobile**.

**Web** is kind of two surfaces, as we have the public facing "app.t3.codes" as well as locally hosting the web app through the `npx t3` command. Both need to be supported by all new features where reasonable.

**Desktop** is the main surface most users install first. It's a full Electron app that bundles the server runner as well. The desktop app can also be used as the host server, allowing remote connections from app.t3.codes or the mobile app.

**Mobile** is a React Native app for both iOS and Android, available on the App Store and Google Play. The mobile app allows for connecting to any T3 Code server to control work remotely.

## A note from Theo

I like ambitious ideas, simple systems, and software that feels obvious. Do not preserve complexity just because it already exists. Do not introduce machinery because it looks architecturally impressive. Understand the real constraint, then fight for the smallest model that makes the correct behavior unsurprising.

Channel both "measure twice, cut once" and "yagni". Fight scope creep. Try to honor the dev's intent in both a minimal and realistic fashion.

The rest of this document is meant to help you navigate the codebase and make changes effectively. Think of these instructions less as "hard rules", more as "good defaults". The developer's preferences should be able to override anything here.

Of note: Most T3 Code contributions will come from T3 Code itself, often controlled remotely. This means you should be careful about accessing data, killing dev servers, and other things that may damage the T3 Code instance that the contributor is using.

## A small glossary

We need to be on the same page with terminology. When communicating, use this language:

- **you** means the agent reading this file and changing T3 Code.
- **we, us, and maintainers** mean Theo, Julius and the people building T3 Code. These are who you are talking to now.
- **user** means the person using T3 Code to direct coding agents.
- **agent** means the coding agent a user runs inside T3 Code. Depending on context, that may also include you.
- **provider** means the agent runtime or harness T3 Code talks to, such as Codex, Claude, Cursor, or OpenCode.
- **client** means the web, desktop, or mobile UI.
- **environment** means one running T3 server and the machine, filesystem, provider credentials, and state it owns.
- **project** means an environment-local workspace record rooted at a directory.
- **thread** means the durable conversation and work history for a project.
- **turn** means one user-to-agent cycle, including follow-up work such as checkpointing.
- **T3 home** means the base data directory. Runtime state normally lives below its userdata directory.

## The three ways to hurt yourself

1. **Killing by pattern.** Never `pkill -f`, `pgrep | kill`, or `kill` a PID you found by matching a name, path, or worktree string. Your own agent process has this worktree's path in its argv, and this machine runs several other dev servers at once. Kill only a PID you captured at spawn, or the owner of your port from `ss -H -ltnp` after confirming `/proc/<pid>/cwd` is your worktree.
2. **Writing to the live install.** `~/.t3/userdata` is the developer's real T3 Code database, in use while you work. Reading it and copying from it are fine, and a good way to get real test data (see Test data). Never start a server against it, never open it read-write, never clean it up.
3. **Baking in origins.** Never set `VITE_HTTP_URL` or `VITE_WS_URL` for dev. Dev is single-origin and Vite proxies `/api`, `/ws`, `/oauth`, and `/.well-known`. Setting them bakes localhost into the bundle and silently breaks every remote browser.

## Hit every surface

The most common defect in this repo is a change that works on the path you tested and is missing everywhere else. Before calling frontend work done, walk this list and say which entries applied:

- **Entry points.** A behavior reachable from the chat view is usually also reachable from Settings, the command palette, and a keybinding. Fixing one is not fixing the feature.
- **Clients.** Web, desktop (wraps web, adds Electron shell/IPC), and mobile (React Native, separate navigation). Shared logic lives in `packages/client-runtime`
- **Providers.** Codex, Claude, Cursor, Grok, OpenCode, and Antigravity each have an adapter. Provider-shaped features need a decision per adapter, even if the decision is "not supported here".
- **Agents.** A capability a user can trigger is usually one an agent should reach through MCP tools, and scheduled tasks run the same paths. That only works when it is a service method, not handler code.
- **Contracts.** Anything crossing the wire is typed in `packages/contracts`. Change the schema and the server, web, mobile, and desktop all follow.
- **Reverse states.** If you added a way in, add the way out and the way to see it. Snooze needs unsnooze. Close needs reopen. A one-way door is a bug.
- **Connection modes.** Local, remote/relay, and tunnel behave differently. Multi-device and multi-environment cases are real.
- **Docs.** Check whether the change makes existing guidance inaccurate. Apply the [documentation rules](#documentation) before adding anything.

## Dev servers

- `vp i` installs. Worktrees get this from the t3.json setup script; if module resolution looks broken, it probably did not run.
- Setup runs in the background. While `.t3/setup-running` names a live PID, wait for it and do not run `vp i`. It ends with `.t3/setup-done` or `.t3/setup-failed` (with the error tail). With no marker at all, setup never ran here, so run `vp i` yourself.
- `vp run dev` starts server and web. In a worktree, state defaults to that worktree's gitignored `.t3`, which deliberately outranks an ambient `T3CODE_HOME` so you cannot land on shared state by accident. An explicit `--home-dir` still wins.
- Ports derive from the worktree path and are stable across restarts, but read the real ones from the `[dev-runner]` line since occupied ports shift.
- Sharing over the tailnet is three steps: run `vp run dev --share` in the background, wait for the `pairingUrl:` line in its output, then give that full URL to an unpaired browser. Do not wire up `tailscale serve` by hand, open the URL yourself, or consume the user's pairing link. A browser with the reusable dev cookie can use the bare origin. If a normal one-time token was consumed, mint a fresh one with `node apps/server/src/bin.ts pair`. It carries standard scopes, while the startup URL carries admin scopes needed for Connections settings.
- To reuse web dev auth across worktrees, configure one fixed `T3CODE_DEV_AUTH_TOKEN` in the main checkout's gitignored `.env`. The `t3.json` setup links that file into worktrees. Never commit or publish the token or a startup URL. See [Reusable dev credential](docs/operations/development.md#reusable-dev-credential).
- Stop what you started, by the PID you tracked. See rule 1.
- Need a second checkout? `git worktree add` it next to this worktree, not in `/tmp`. Remove it when done.

## Test data

An empty database is a bad test. Seed your worktree's `.t3` with a copy of real data instead of pointing at live state:

- The first `vp run dev` in a worktree does this for you when its database is missing and the source is at most 500 MiB. Larger sources warn and dev starts with an empty database. `--no-seed` or `T3CODE_DEV_SEED=0` skips seeding. Manual migration still accepts larger sources and may use substantial disk space before pruning.
- Run `vp run migrate-dev-db` with your dev server stopped to refresh. It rebuilds `<worktree>/.t3/userdata/statev2.sqlite` from a read-only snapshot of `~/.t3/userdata/statev2.sqlite`, the developer's real data. It keeps recent projects and their stopped threads, and drops scheduled tasks, pending work, and auth sessions, so your dev server never runs the developer's agents. Raise `--projects` and `--threads-per-project` for more data.
- Refresh `statev2.sqlite`, not `state.sqlite`. The server copies the V1 `state.sqlite` only when `statev2.sqlite` is missing.
- Bring `secrets` and `settings.json` only if the flow under test needs them.
- Copy in, never symlink. Data flows one way: into your sandbox, never back out.

## Verifying

- Before you push, run `vp run check:changed`. It runs CI's fast checks for changed files: format, lint, knip, typecheck of affected packages and dependents, and tests beside changes. CI still runs the full test suites.
- While you iterate, run `vp test run <files>`. For big files, add `-t "<name>"`.
- Use `vp run typecheck`, not `npx tsc`; it caches per package. Both run tsc-rs (`typescript` is the `@tsc-rs/typescript` drop-in).
- Run `node -e` snippets from `apps/server` or the owning package. `effect` does not resolve from the repo root.
- Test behavior that can break, such as orchestration and event-sourcing, provider protocol translation, auth and permission guards, persistence and migrations, external-format parsing, race fixes, and the logic a bug fix changed. Leave out tests for what types already guarantee, trivial logic, copy text, smoke runs, mock-call mirrors, callback wiring, and props rendered to static markup.
- Extend before you add. When an existing test or table covers the behavior, add a row or an assertion there. Write a new `it` only when no case fits.
- Test at one layer: the lowest one that fails on `main`. Do not repeat the case in a wrapper test, at each call site, or in web and mobile copies of the same logic.
- [Testing](docs/internals/testing.md) carries these same test rules, plus review guidance, for review bots. Change both together.
- **Do not run repo-wide checks.** No `vp check`, no `vp run -r test`, no `vp run -r typecheck` unless I ask. CI owns the full suite.
- Backend behavior changes ship with focused tests for that behavior.
- Proof for a bug fix depends on the bug. Logic, data, state, and protocol bugs get a failing test first (the fewest that fail on `main` for that reason, in an existing case of the module's test file where one fits), then the fix. Purely visual bugs (spacing, colour, alignment, a layout shift) get before/after captures as their proof and no test: do not add UI tests for nitpicks, and do not ask for one in review when a capture already shows it. A server-only fix with no visible surface ships the test plus a short runtime transcript.
- The server is event-sourced, and side effects run after the command commits. In tests, drain the effect worker (`OrchestrationEffectWorkerV2.drain`) or await the specific persisted event or `Deferred` that marks the milestone. Never wait on sleeps or polling. A test that needs a timeout to pass is wrong. Concretely:
  - `it.effect` runs on a `TestClock`; `Effect.sleep` only advances through `TestClock.adjust`. `it.live` is wall-clock and only for subprocess or network fixtures.
  - No `yieldNow` or `sleep` polling loops. Await the `Deferred`, take from the `Queue`, or drain the worker.
  - No per-test timeout argument or `retry`. The project timeout is the ceiling, and flaky tests are fixed, not retried.
  - No `performance.now()` or `Date.now()` deltas. Assert on events and counts, not elapsed time.
  - Browser tests assert through `expect.element` or `vi.waitFor`, never `requestAnimationFrame` or `transitionend`.
  - `vi.mock` factories must not spread a real module that pulls in Shiki or the diff workers.
  - `it.skip` and friends need a tracking issue on the line above: `// quarantine: #1234 <why>`.
  - Lint enforces this: `t3code/no-test-timeout-or-unreasoned-skip`, `t3code/no-frame-waits-in-browser-tests`, `t3code/no-wall-clock-in-tests`, `t3code/no-real-time-wait-in-tests`, `t3code/no-polling-loop-in-tests`.
- Web browser tests are `*.browser.test.tsx` or `*.browser.test.ts` and render with `await using screen = await render(...)` from `apps/web/test/render.tsx`. `t3code/require-disposable-render` errors on the old patterns.
  - Acquire what the test drives after mounting (fake timers it advances, spies it sets up after mounting) after the render, so it disposes before the unmount. Anything the first render reads comes before it.
  - A helper that renders and then waits or clicks puts the screen in an `AsyncDisposableStack` and `move()`s it out only on success, so a failed wait still unmounts.
  - `rerender` needs a fresh element on every call.
  - No lifecycle hooks and no module-level mutable state. Shared mock state that `vi.mock` factories read is reset by a `setup()` call at the top of the test.
  - `router` is on by default. Pass `router: false` only with a one-line comment saying why.

  ```tsx
  it("saves on Enter", async () => {
    const onSave = vi.fn();
    using _now = vi.spyOn(Date, "now").mockReturnValue(0);
    await using screen = await render(<TitleEditor onSave={onSave} />, { router: "/threads/1" });
    await userEvent.type(screen.getByRole("textbox"), "Title{Enter}");
    expect(onSave).toHaveBeenCalledWith("Title");
  });
  ```

- Upon request, user-visible frontend changes should get one integrated pass in a real client: `test-t3-app` for web, `test-t3-mobile` for mobile. The primary agent does this once after integrating. Subagents do not launch their own dev servers. Ask permission before doing computer use or spinning up browsers.

- Real agent turns cost money. To watch a turn stream through the pipeline and UI, use the free `Replay (dev)` provider that `vp run dev` registers; [test-t3-app](.agents/skills/test-t3-app/SKILL.md) shows how to start one. Use a real provider only when the change depends on that provider's behavior, and then pick its cheapest model, such as Haiku for Claude or Luna for Codex.

For authorized mobile verification, a missing or outdated native client is an install step, not a blocker. Run `vp run mobile:install <ios|android> [device-id]` on the device host before starting Metro; it targets the only booted simulator or connected Android device when the id is omitted. It installs the dev client for this checkout's native fingerprint from the shared cache in seconds and builds only when no machine has built it yet, so prefer it over `expo run:*`, `xcodebuild`, or `gradlew`, which rebuild from scratch. Its stdout is one JSON line; build output goes to the log it names. See `test-t3-mobile` for the full workflow.

## Evals

`evals/` checks how real models behave with T3 Code's model-facing text: agent instructions, MCP tool descriptions and schemas, and generated titles. Before you change that text, read [evals/README.md](evals/README.md) and run the evals it names. When you fix a model behavior bug, add a case that fails before the fix.

## Pull requests

- Never make a PR unless the developer explicitly asks you to do so.
- If `origin` is git.cafe, follow [GitCafe mirror](docs/operations/development.md#gitcafe-mirror-optional): push to `origin`, open and track PRs with `cafe` and their git.cafe URLs, and keep `gh` for merging.
- Conventional commit titles, plain language: `fix(web): new threads no longer spike CPU`.
- Body: the problem in a sentence or two, then how you fixed it. End with the model and harness that did the work.
- UI changes need before/after images. Motion or timing needs a short video.
- Upload PR evidence to GitHub. Never commit PR-only screenshots or assets such as `.github/pr-assets/`.
- One request is one PR. Split it only when the maintainer asks. Outside contributions follow the stricter [one problem per PR](CONTRIBUTING.md#one-problem) rule.
- When babysitting: call `watch_pull_request` and end your turn. T3 Code wakes you on checks, comments, or conflicts. Do not poll or sleep. Verify each bot finding against the source, fix real ones, dismiss false positives with a written reason. Stay quiet when nothing is new. Stop when the bots are green on the latest commit.

## Documentation

Most code changes do not need an internal documentation change. Agents can read the code.

- `docs/internals/` is for architectural decisions and their reasons, constraints that span components, and implementation traps that are hard to discover from the source. Before adding a paragraph, ask what a maintainer would get wrong without it. If reading the relevant code answers the question, leave it out.
- Do not document every feature, enumerate fields or methods, narrate control flow, maintain file catalogs, or append PR summaries. Types, tests, and code already record the implementation. The glossary defines shared vocabulary; it is not a feature index.
- A local reason the code can't show goes in a short nearby code comment. Use an internal doc when the reasoning crosses boundaries or needs context the code cannot carry well. Link to the relevant source instead of copying it.
- When a documented decision or constraint changes, rewrite or remove the affected text. Do not append another account of the new behavior. A new internal page needs a distinct, durable reason to exist.
- `docs/user/` helps users accomplish tasks. Give each major feature a concise section explaining what it does, how to start, and anything unintuitive. A settings path is useful; descriptions of visible buttons, icons, layouts, animations, or every UI state are not. Before adding text, ask what task or decision it helps the user with.
- Keep user docs in the shipped product's voice, without implementation details or contributor tooling. Update the relevant feature section when how to use it changes. A UI tweak does not need a documentation entry, and a new control does not need its own page.
- `docs/operations/` holds maintainer setup, release, and debugging procedures. Keep instructions for operating an installed T3 Code server in the user guides.

## Plans and work artifacts

- Do not commit implementation plans, research notes, or agent scratch files. Keep temporary working material outside the worktree. `.plans/` is gitignored only as a safety net for legacy tooling.
- Track active maintainer work in the GitHub issue or project item that owns it. External proposals follow `CONTRIBUTING.md` and belong in Ideas discussions.
- A merged PR is the implementation record. Close or update its tracking item when the work lands; do not preserve a second checklist in the repository.

## How it works

Clients send typed WebSocket requests. The server turns them into _commands_. The _orchestrator_ (`apps/server/src/orchestration-v2/Orchestrator.ts`) serializes commands and decides _events_ without doing any I/O. The _event sink_ commits those events, the _projections_ the UI reads, the _command receipt_, and _outbox_ effects in one transaction. The _effect worker_ then runs the effects, such as starting a provider turn or capturing a checkpoint, and feeds results back as commands. Provider CLIs run as subprocesses; per-provider _adapters_ translate their native protocols into orchestration events. Each turn ends with a _checkpoint_, a hidden git ref, so the app can diff and restore.

Architecture and its constraints: `docs/internals/overview.md`. Glossary: `docs/internals/glossary.md`

## Where code lives

- `apps/server` - WebSocket, orchestration, providers, checkpointing. Effect-heavy: read [Effect services](docs/internals/effect-services.md) before adding server code, and `.repos/effect-smol/LLMS.md` for the Effect library itself.
- `apps/web` - React/Vite UI. `apps/desktop` wraps it, `apps/mobile` is React Native, `apps/marketing` is the site.
- `packages/contracts` - Effect/Schema contracts plus small derived helpers. No heavy runtime logic.
- `packages/shared` - shared runtime utils, subpath exports, no barrel.
- `packages/client-runtime` - client code shared by web and mobile.
- `.repos/` - vendored read-only references. Prefer their patterns over invented ones. Never edit or import from them. Sync with `vpr sync:repos` when bumping the matching dependency. If it is missing (sparse checkout), read a file with `git show origin/main:.repos/<path>`.

## Taste

- Complexity belongs at the adapter boundary. Orchestration stays pure, UI stays dumb.
- Client mutations use `createEnvironmentRpcCommand`. Add protected methods to `CLIENT_GUARDED_RPC_SCOPES` in contracts and use the command's `permissionAtom` for UI availability. Grants are checked at execution against the destination environment; the server remains authoritative. Keep raw RPC clients inside `rpc/`, and extend the permission behavior tests when adding a protected method.
- Server features are services; transports stay thin. A `ws.ts` RPC handler, HTTP route, or MCP tool decodes input, calls one service method, and maps errors. See [Effect services](docs/internals/effect-services.md).
- `apps/web/src/components/ui` exports own their look. Pick a `variant` or `size`; do not restyle one with `className`. If none fits and the look is a generic concept, add a variant to the component; a look that belongs to one feature stays in that feature's own component, not in `components/ui`. Layout classes (width, flex, margin, position) belong on the parent. `shadcn/no-restyle` fails lint on violations. See [Web UI](docs/internals/web-ui.md).
- Reusable Effect functions use `Effect.fn("Service.operation")` with a stable span name, not a
  function wrapping `Effect.gen`. Keep `Effect.gen` for inline programs and layer construction.
  Use `Effect.fnUntraced` only when spans would be too frequent (stream chunks, per-event
  projection, tight loops) or duplicate an existing tracing boundary; explain that choice nearby.
  Named `Effect.fn` creates a span; the unnamed form does not. Preserve existing span names and
  options, and pass combinators as additional function-builder arguments.
- Inferred types over annotations. `any` is the enemy.
- Default to no comment. Write one only for a constraint, an external quirk, or an invariant the code can't show, in one line where you can and four at most. Don't restate names or signatures, narrate steps, record history, or explain the fix you just made; the PR carries that. `t3code/no-low-value-comments` enforces the length cap and the mechanical cases.
- React effects are for synchronizing with something outside React. Derive in render and act in handlers instead of syncing state, but don't hide real lifecycle work in refs or stores to dodge one. The `t3code/no-unreasoned-state-sync` lint rule reports every effect; one that stays states its reason with `// oxlint-disable-next-line t3code/no-unreasoned-state-sync -- <why>`.
- Our users drive agents all day and notice a dropped frame, a lying spinner, and a stale label. No continuously repainting animations; they peg the GPU on high-refresh displays.
- If a rule here fights the task in front of you, say so loudly and get a human sign-off before breaking it.

## Additional tips

- Don't verify with browsers or computer use unless the user explicitly agrees or requests it.
- Security is important, but should not be over-indexed on, especially for dev mode/maintainer-only features.

content.text:
Our AGENTS.md is clearly forked from t3code's. The section order and much of the wording match. The differences come from swapping in inkling's product and dropping the parts that only fit a multi-surface, remote, Effect-based monorepo.

## What's the same

- **Structure:** intro → what makes it special → a note on taste → glossary → three ways to hurt yourself → hit every surface → dev servers → test data → verifying → PRs → docs → plans → how it works → where code lives → taste → tips.
- **Rules carried over almost verbatim:**
  - Never kill by pattern.
  - Never write to the live data.
  - Don't run repo-wide checks.
  - One request is one PR.
  - Conventional commit titles.
  - PR evidence goes to GitHub.
  - Don't commit plans.
  - Keep docs minimal.
  - Inferred types over `any`.
  - No continuously repainting animations.
  - Comments only where code can't show the reason.
  - A rule that fights the task needs a human sign-off.

## Product values

| | t3code | inkling |
|---|---|---|
| Pillars | Open at the core, performance, remote ready, multi-surface | Instant capture, performance, local first forever, quiet intelligence, visual by type |
| Emphasis | Distribution and architecture (forks, tunnels, three clients) | User trust and feel (never lose data, no network, AI stays invisible) |
| Intro voice | "A note from Theo", names Theo and Julius, cites 500k users | "A note on taste", no named people |

Performance is in both, but inkling's version targets different failures: full content over IPC, ungrouped card grids, and blocking capture on OCR or embeddings.

## Sections that differ in substance

- **Hurting yourself, rule 3:** t3code's is about `VITE_HTTP_URL`/`VITE_WS_URL` baking an origin into the bundle. Ours is broader: no hardcoded ports, user paths or model cache paths, and never commit databases, models, embeddings, benchmark output or secrets. Ours also gives Windows commands (`Get-NetTCPConnection`, `Win32_Process`) where theirs uses `ss` and `/proc`.
- **Hit every surface:**
  - t3code lists Clients, Providers, Agents/MCP, Contracts and Connection modes.
  - We list Capture paths, Search paths, Card types and App modes (preview vs full app).
  - Both keep Entry points, Reverse states and Docs.
- **Dev servers and test data:**
  - t3code's are far more automated: setup markers, worktree-derived ports, `--share` over the tailnet, a reusable dev auth token, and an auto-seeding `migrate-dev-db` script that prunes scheduled tasks and sessions.
  - Ours is manual: use SQLite backup semantics, copy only the assets you need, and prefer the committed `public/seed-demo/`.
  - Ours adds the Bun version pin, keeping `t3.json` in sync, and "never `Start-Sleep` after launching a server".
- **Verifying:**
  - t3code's is much longer. It covers `vp run check:changed`, test layering and "extend before you add", the proof required for each kind of bug fix, the `TestClock` and `Deferred` rules, five named lint rules, and the browser-test `await using screen` pattern.
  - Ours is shorter: a list of what earns a test, the same no-sleeps stance but without the lint rules, and "a behavior change with no test is unfinished".
  - **Real-app testing is a notable disagreement.** Ours requires one real pass in the running app with a screenshot for UI changes. Theirs makes that opt-in and says to ask permission before using browsers or computer use.
- **Sections only t3code has:**
  - Evals for model-facing text.
  - Mobile install and verification.
  - The git.cafe mirror.
  - The Effect conventions in Taste (`Effect.fn`, thin transports, `createEnvironmentRpcCommand`, `shadcn/no-restyle`, the React-effect lint rule).
- **Sections only we have:**
  - Linear issues workflow.
  - Changelog rules, including "never write that an agent did the work".
  - "Working in this harness" (screenshot paths).
  - A security note about untrusted fetched HTML.
  - "Capture paths stay fast and forgiving".
- **Docs layout:** theirs is `docs/internals/`, `docs/user/` and `docs/operations/`. Ours is `product.md`, `product-behavior.md`, `tech-stack.md`, `roadmap.md` and `changelog.md`, plus `docs/operations/`.
- **How it works and where code lives:** theirs describes the event-sourced orchestrator, outbox, projections and checkpoints in a monorepo (`apps/`, `packages/`, `.repos/`). Ours describes capture, then jobs with leases, then FTS triggers, in a single package (`src/`, `electron/`).

## Gaps in ours

1. **No mention of Effect.** The Electron backend uses Effect in 17 files, and the recent "Effect backend with typed IPC contracts" commit (#187) landed it. AGENTS.md has no guidance on services, `Effect.fn`, or the typed IPC contracts, though t3code's has all three.
2. **Babysitting advice is stale.** Ours says "poll checks and comments". t3code's says to call `watch_pull_request`, end the turn, and never poll, which matches how this harness works.
3. **The tracker is described inconsistently.**
   - "Plans and work artifacts" still says "the GitHub issue or project item" (inherited from t3code).
   - The Linear section says the Linear issue is the tracker, "not `roadmap.md`", and then also says to tick the `roadmap.md` box.
   - That also sits awkwardly with "don't keep a second checklist".

I made the three edits to `AGENTS.md`.

- **Bun version:** The pin itself has to stay. CI's `bun-version-file`, `packageManager` and `check:bun-version` all depend on it. What we didn't need was the hardcoded `1.4.2` in AGENTS.md, which is already repeated in README, CONTRIBUTING and `development.md`. The line now reads "If module resolution looks broken, run `bun run check:bun-version`."
- **Changelog rule:** I removed the "keep `docs/changelog.md` current… ask the developer…" bullet under Plans and work artifacts. I took that to be the one you added. The bullet under Documentation is still there. It restates the file's own header and has the "never write that an agent did the work" line. Say so if that's the one you meant, or if you want both gone.
- **Screenshot note:** I removed the whole "Working in this harness" section. Once the screenshot bullet was gone, only a one-line browser note was left. The Verifying section still says "Take a screenshot through the harness so the user can see it," which still reads fine.

## What to take from t3code

1. **Effect conventions.** The Electron backend uses Effect in 17 files since #187, and AGENTS.md doesn't mention it. A short Taste bullet plus a pointer to a doc would do. I'd read `electron/` first so it describes what the code actually does. I wouldn't copy t3code's `Effect.fn` rules without checking that we follow them.
2. **Bug-fix proof rules.** Logic, data and protocol bugs get a failing test first. Purely visual bugs get before/after captures and no test. Our "a behavior change with no test is unfinished" is blunt and would push agents to write the UI tests we say not to write.
3. **"Extend before you add" and "test at one layer."** Add a row or assertion to an existing test before writing a new one, and test at the lowest layer that fails. Together they keep the suite from growing.
4. **A named "check changed files" script.** Ours says "targeted lint and typecheck" without a command. t3code points at one, `vp run check:changed`. If we don't have an equivalent, a small script would save agents from guessing.
5. **Babysitting.** Replace "poll checks and comments" with "call `watch_pull_request` and end your turn." That matches how this harness works.
6. **A pointer to the `verify-inkling` skill** from the UI-verification rule. t3code does the same with `test-t3-app`, and the skill already exists here.
7. **Lint enforcement for test rules.** Our no-sleeps and no-wall-clock rules are prose only, while t3code backs the same ones with lint rules. If `oxlint-plugin-inkling` can enforce them, that is more reliable than prose.

I wouldn't take the remote, mobile, evals, git.cafe, dev-auth or `--share` material, because none of it applies here. The `migrate-dev-db` script is optional. It would replace a lot of test-data prose, but only if you find yourselves re-seeding often.

## General improvements

- **Tracker contradictions.**
  - "Plans and work artifacts" still says "GitHub issue or project item," but Linear is the tracker.
  - The Linear section says the issue is the tracker "not `roadmap.md`" and then tells agents to tick the `roadmap.md` box.
  - "Don't keep a second checklist" sits awkwardly with that box too.
  - Pick one source of truth and rewrite the three spots to match.
- **Rot-prone specifics.** "Where code lives" has "the 48 item corpus," and the `docs/` line is a file catalog, which our own docs rule says not to keep. Both go stale quietly.
- **Duplicated rule.** "If a rule here fights the task, say so" appears in the intro and again at the end of Taste. Keep one.
- **Typos:** "abitrary" (line 3), "execption" and "animations(with" (the mascot line).
- **"Hit every surface."** Say which entries apply to which kind of change. A pure UI tweak doesn't need Capture paths or Search paths. Otherwise agents will recite the whole list every time.

## Effect in the main process

The main process is built on [Effect](https://effect.website) so leases, timeouts, retries, and shutdown come from one tested runtime instead of hand-rolled timers and flags. `electron/main.ts` builds a single `ManagedRuntime` holding the library, the job queue, and two workers; quitting disposes it, which interrupts running jobs and hands them back as pending. Each job kind has a timeout in `electron/ai-jobs.ts`, so a hung model or decoder fails its job instead of stalling the queue. Effect stops at the IPC edge: handlers call storage through a Promise facade, and the renderer never imports Effect at runtime.

URL ingestion downloads through Effect's HTTP client, which retries rate limits, gateway errors, and dropped connections, waits at least as long as a `Retry-After` header asks, and stays inside the 15-second capture budget. Redirects stay manual so each hop passes the private-network check before it is followed.

# Babysit PR

Many repos have AI review bots. They're helpful, even if they are not always
right.

## Waiting

Never write your own watcher, polling loop, or `sleep` loop. Use one watcher
per PR: `watch_pull_request` in T3 Code, `pr-wait` everywhere else. Never run
both on the same PR. Every watcher on a GitHub account shares one rate limit.

### In T3 Code: `watch_pull_request`

Handle the existing checks and comments first. Then call
`watch_pull_request` and end your turn. T3 Code wakes you with a message when
a check fails, the required checks pass, someone comments or reviews, or the
branch conflicts.

- **Only the thread that owns the PR watches it.** If you are a delegated
  child task (a reviewer, a Sol round, any `delegate_task` child), never call
  `watch_pull_request`. The parent owns the PR. Do not watch PRs you are not
  working on.
- **A wake is news, not a merge decision.** Check the merge gate yourself.
- **Unwatch when you hand off.** A watched thread stays in Working and out of
  the user's inbox. When you stop (ready, blocked, or asking the user a question),
  call `unwatch_pull_request` first. A merge or close ends the watch on its
  own.
- **"Stopped watching, could not read it"** usually means GitHub's rate limit
  is used up. Run `gh api rate_limit --jq .resources.graphql` before you
  watch again. If `remaining` is near 0, wait for `reset` with one background
  command, then watch again. Never watch again in a tight loop.

### Everywhere else: `pr-wait`

Wait with `scripts/pr-wait` from this skill's directory (use its absolute
path).

```bash
pr-wait <pr> [--repo owner/name] [--until ready|green|any-change]
```

It prints one line per real event. It exits 0 when the `--until` condition is
met or the PR merges, 1 when it needs you (a required check failed, conflicts,
unresolved threads, PR closed), and 2 on bad input.

- `ready` (default): required checks green, Greptile or Macroscope reviewed the
  head, and no unresolved threads. Use this to babysit.
- `green`: required checks only. Use it when the repo has no Greptile or
  Macroscope.
- `any-change`: exit on the first event.

In Claude Code, run it with the Monitor tool (`timeout_ms: 3600000`), so each
line wakes you. Without a monitor, run it as one long command. It ends on its
own.

Start it again after you push, after you handle an exit 1, and after a resume.
It remembers what it already reported, so nothing that arrived in between is
lost. If it says another pid already watches the PR, do not start a second one.
Kill the old one only if its events do not reach you.

With either watcher: when an event needs no action, end your turn without a
message. Never post or say "still waiting".

## GitHub rate limits

`gh pr create`, `gh pr view`, and `gh pr checks` use GraphQL. When GraphQL is
used up, the REST limit is separate and usually still has room. Use
`gh api repos/<owner>/<repo>/pulls/<n>` to read a PR, and
`gh api repos/<owner>/<repo>/commits/<sha>/check-runs` for checks.

## Reviews

Only act on checks and comments newer than the latest push. Verify every bot
finding against the source before changing code. Fix real findings and CI
failures, distinguish repository failures from infrastructure flakes, and reply
with a written reason when dismissing false positives.

If the repo has `.macroscope/check-run-agents/*.md`, read those rules before you
reply to a Macroscope finding. Its findings cite them.

CodeRabbit is advisory. Treat its findings like any other finding, but never
wait for it and never hold a merge for it.

If a review bot leaves feedback you believe is not worth addressing, reply with
a written reason and resolve the comment. Use the `leaving-pr-comments` skill
for every comment posted on the user's behalf.

Screenshots and videos help as well, when you have a way to upload them.

Keep the PR at the size the user's goal needs. Review loops tend to grow a
PR one cheap-looking fix at a time. Fix real bugs in the intended case.
Decline the rest with a written reason, and list them as follow-ups:
unneeded tests, guards for edge cases that do not matter, extra integration
or compatibility, and small performance costs. Prefer the fix that deletes or
narrows code.

## Base branch and merging

Keep an eye on changes to `main` and rebase when needed. `pr-wait` reports when
new base commits touch this PR's files, and when the PR becomes BEHIND or DIRTY.
`watch_pull_request` reports conflicts only, so check for BEHIND yourself
before you call the PR ready.
If an overlapping PR makes this one obsolete, stop monitoring, report it to the
user, and ask before closing the PR unless closure was explicitly authorized.

If nothing has changed, stay quiet rather than posting filler comments. Stop
when `pr-wait` exits 0, or in T3 Code when the merge gate passes on the latest
head. Merge only when the user explicitly requested it;
otherwise report that the PR is ready. Right before a merge, run `git fetch` and
check the PR again. Never merge when it is BEHIND or DIRTY, or when base commits
that landed after the last green run touch this PR's files. Rebase, push, and
